title: 22. Interview: Design Chat Application
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Chat Application — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Chat Application interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events vs long-polling**: WS chosen for bidirectional (typing, acks). SSE would suffice for receive-only, but typing uplink is awkward.
- **REST send + WS receive vs WS-only**: REST send gives us HTTP-level idempotency (`Idempotency-Key`), easier retries, and decouples send-path from receive-path. Slack and Discord both use REST send + WS receive.
- **Postgres + Citus vs Cassandra for messages**: Citus gives us per-conversation transactional `seq_id` cheaply and ad-hoc SQL for analytics. Cassandra's log-structured storage is great for append-only but read-receipt updates are read-modify-write heavy. We chose Postgres for consistency; Cassandra would be the pick at >100 M msg/day.
- **Kafka partition by `conv_id` vs `user_id`**: `conv_id` keeps per-conversation order naturally; `user_id` would scatter a conversation's messages across partitions and require merging.
- **Push gateway per-region vs centralised**: Per-region reduces mobile RTT but complicates ops. We use centralised with regional FCM/APNs endpoints.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. How do you guarantee message ordering in a group chat with 200 members?
**Answer:** Ordering is per-conversation, not global. We partition Kafka by `conversation_id`, so all messages for one conversation land on the same partition and are consumed in order by a single fan-out worker (per partition). The `seq_id` is assigned by Postgres on the write path using a per-conversation sequence (`nextval('seq_'||conv_id)`), guaranteed monotonic within the transaction. Clients display messages ordered by `seq_id`; if a higher `seq_id` arrives before a lower one (rare network reordering on the WebSocket), the client buffers for 200 ms and renders in order. For hot conversations exceeding a single partition's throughput, we shard by `msg_id` within the conversation and re-stitch using `seq_id` at the gateway — complexity we accept only when needed.
**Visual:**
```
Producer -> Kafka partition = hash(conv_id) % 200
                |
                v
       single fan-out worker (in-order consume)
                |
                v
   Deliver (seq_id) --> clients sort by seq_id
```

### Q2. How would you handle a single user connected from 5 devices simultaneously?
**Answer:** The Session Registry maps `user_id → {device_id: server_id:conn_id}` (a Redis HASH), so each device gets its own entry. When a message is fanned out, we look up all of the user's device entries and deliver to each. Read receipts are per-device in Redis but consolidated to a per-user `last_read_seq` in Postgres (the max across devices). Sending a message from one device echoes it to the user's other devices (via a separate `self_devices` Kafka topic) so all UIs stay in sync. Presence is per-user (not per-device): online if any device has a recent heartbeat. Token refresh and reconnection are device-scoped. This mirrors WhatsApp/iMessage multi-device behavior.
**Visual:**
```
user_id 42:
  device web   -> gw5:connA
  device ios   -> gw9:connB
  device mac   -> gw5:connC
fan-out -> deliver to connA, connB, connC
```

### Q3. How does presence scale to 50 M users with avg 50 contacts each?
**Answer:** Naive fan-out would emit 2.5 B presence updates/day. We use three tricks: (1) **Hysteresis** — only publish state transitions (online↔offline), not every heartbeat. Heartbeats just refresh `last_seen` silently. (2) **Subscriber pull on-demand** — when a user opens their contacts list, we batch-fetch presence for visible contacts via `MGET`. We do not push presence for all 50 contacts continuously. (3) **Interest-based pub/sub** — a user subscribes to presence updates only for their actively-open conversations (typically < 20). With these, presence traffic drops to ~100 M events/day. A background sweeper marks users offline if no heartbeat for 60 s, using a Redis ZSET indexed by `last_seen` timestamp for efficient range scans.
**Visual:**
```
heartbeat (every 10s) -> SET presence:{uid} = now   (silent)
sweeper (every 5s)    -> ZRANGEBYSCORE presence_index 0 (now-60s)
                        -> for each stale uid: PUBLISH presence:{uid} "offline"
client opens conv     -> MGET presence:{u1,u2,...,u20}
```

### Q4. What happens if a user is offline when a message is sent to them?
**Answer:** The fan-out worker looks up the user in the Session Registry; on miss (or stale TTL), the user is marked offline. The message is already durably stored in Postgres with its `seq_id`. The worker enqueues a push-notification job to a separate Kafka topic `push_jobs`. The Push Service batches pushes per device-token (max 1000 tokens/batch for FCM) and calls FCM/APNs. When the user's app comes online, it opens a WebSocket, sends `GET /messages?since_seq={last_known}` and pulls any missed messages from Postgres (or Redis hot cache). The push notification's `data.payload` includes the `msg_id` so deep-linking works. Push is best-effort — the source of truth is the database, so even if FCM drops the push, the user sees the message on next open.
**Visual:**
```
offline user:
  msg -> Postgres (durable)
       -> Kafka push_jobs
       -> Push Service -> FCM/APNs -> device
  device online later -> WS connect -> GET /messages?since_seq=N -> Postgres replay
```

### Q5. How do you implement read receipts without overwhelming the database?
**Answer:** Each `POST /messages/{id}/read` updates `read_receipts (conv_id, user_id, last_read_seq)`. To avoid one write per message, the client batches: it sends a single receipt update per conversation per 5-second window, with the highest `seq_id` it has read. The Postgres update is a single `UPSERT` per (conv_id, user_id) — only one row per user per conversation ever exists, so the table stays small (50 M users × avg 50 convs = 2.5 B rows — Citus-distributed). Read-receipt fan-out to the sender goes through Kafka `receipts` topic (partitioned by conv_id), so the sender gets "all 5 members read up to seq 42" updates batched. We render "Read by 4/5" in the UI by comparing each member's `last_read_seq` to the message's `seq_id`.
**Visual:**
```
client reads seq 42 -> 5s debounce -> UPSERT receipts (conv=7, user=me, last_read_seq=42)
                                    -> Kafka receipts partition=hash(7)
                                    -> fan-out -> sender UI: "Read by N"
```

### Q6. How would you design message search across 90 days of history?
**Answer:** We stream messages from Postgres to Elasticsearch via Debezium CDC on the `messages` table (one ES index per workspace, or one per 10 M messages). The ES document has `conv_id`, `sender_id`, `body`, `created_at`, `workspace_id`. Search query: `GET /search?q=release-notes&workspace_id=W&conv_ids=...`. We use ES `match_phrase` with highlighting. Indexing lag is < 1 s. For 5 B msg/day × 90 days = 450 B docs, we shard ES heavily (~100 shards × 50 GB each) and use time-based indices (daily) so old indices can be moved to warm nodes or dropped. We only index text messages, not media (media search uses metadata in Postgres). Per-workspace ACL filters ensure users can't search conversations they've left.
**Visual:**
```
Postgres messages --Debezium CDC--> Kafka cdc.messages --ES Sink--> ES index msgs_2025_11_29
Search API: bool { must:[match_phrase], filter:[term:workspace_id, terms:conv_id] }
```

### Q7. How do you prevent message loss if the Chat Gateway crashes mid-delivery?
**Answer:** The sender's `POST /messages` returns 200 only after Postgres commit + Kafka produce-ack (acks=all, min ISR=2). So by the time we attempt delivery, the message is durable. The fan-out worker consumes from Kafka with **at-least-once** semantics — it commits the offset only after all online recipients have been delivered-to or re-queued. If the worker crashes mid-batch, Kafka replays the uncommitted offsets. Idempotency on the delivery side: the gateway dedupes incoming `Deliver` calls by `(msg_id, conn_id)` (a 60 s LRU cache per connection), so a replayed message won't render twice. For the sender's optimistic UI: if the REST call fails (network blip before 200), the client retries with the same `Idempotency-Key` and the Message Service returns the original `msg_id`. Net result: no message loss, occasional duplicate suppressed.
**Visual:**
```
client POST /messages (idempotency-key=k1)
  -> Postgres commit
  -> Kafka acks=all
  -> return 200 {msg_id}
fan-out worker consumes, delivers, then commits Kafka offset
  crash -> replay offset -> gateway dedupes by (msg_id, conn_id)
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A celebrity opens a public channel with 1 M subscribers and sends "Hello". How do you fan out?
**Answer:** 1 M recipients × 1 message is a broadcast — different from 1:1 chat. We treat channels with > 10 k subscribers as "broadcast channels" and switch strategy. The message is written to Postgres once. Instead of fanning out per-recipient, we use a **fan-out-on-read** approach: subscribers don't get a WebSocket push; instead, their client, on opening the app, fetches the channel's latest messages via REST (cached at CDN edge for public channels). For online subscribers, we batch the push into a single WebSocket notification `{"type": "channel_update", "conv_id": C}` — the client then issues a `GET /messages` to fetch the actual content. This caps server work at O(1) per message + O(online_subscribers) lightweight pings. Push notifications for offline users are batched per device-token (FCM allows 1000 tokens/batch) and rate-limited (we coalesce 10 channel updates into one push). Telegram uses a similar strategy for its 1 M-subscriber channels.
**Visual:**
```
celebrity -> msg -> Postgres (1 row)
                 -> WS ping to online subscribers: "conv C has new msg"
                 -> offline: batched push (1 push per device per 5 min)
subscriber client -> GET /messages?conv=C&since=N  (CDN cached)
```

### Q2. A user reports messages arriving out of order in a 50-member group chat. How do you diagnose?
**Answer:** First, ask the user for screenshots showing two messages with `seq_id`s A and B where B rendered before A but B > A. Check: (1) Did the client buffer? Our client code is supposed to buffer 200 ms and sort by `seq_id`. If the client rendered immediately, that's a client bug. (2) Check Kafka offset monotonicity for that partition — `kafka-consumer-offset-checker` should show sequential consumption. (3) Check if the fan-out worker crashed and replayed — gateway dedupe cache should have caught the duplicate, but if dedup TTL (60 s) expired before the replay, the same `msg_id` could render twice in different positions. (4) Check multi-device: the user may be on two devices with different `last_seq` — one device ahead of the other. (5) Clock skew — `created_at` is wall-clock and can drift, but ordering is by `seq_id`, not `created_at`. If the client is sorting by `created_at` instead of `seq_id`, that's the bug. Fix: enforce client-side sort by `seq_id` and add a regression test.
**Visual:**
```
Investigation:
 1. client sort key (seq_id, not created_at)
 2. Kafka partition order preserved?
 3. fan-out worker replay? dedupe TTL?
 4. multi-device last_seq divergence?
 5. gateway deliver latency variance (slow gateway delayed one msg)
```

### Q3. Black Friday: a customer-support team uses your chat for live support. Traffic spikes 5×. What breaks first?
**Answer:** The first bottleneck is typically the **fan-out worker** Kafka consumer lag, because group fan-out is O(members) per message and members grow with team size. Check `consumer_lag` on the `messages` topic — if it exceeds 10 k, messages are queuing. Auto-scale consumer group by adding worker pods (Kafka rebalances partitions). Second bottleneck: **gateway connection count** — if 5× more users connect, gateway memory spikes. Pre-provision 2× gateway capacity during the predicted window and set autoscale on connection count. Third: **Redis Session Registry** — at 5× presence updates, Redis CPU hits 80 %. Scale Redis Cluster by resharding (online operation). Fourth: **Postgres write throughput** on hot shards — if one workspace dominates, Citus can't help if all its conversations hash to one shard; we'd need to re-shard by `(workspace_id, conv_id)` to spread load. Fifth: **push notifications** rate-limited at FCM/APNs — pre-negotiate higher quotas with providers. Mitigation: circuit-breaker that downgrades to email digest if push queue > 1 M.
**Visual:**
```
traffic 5x:
 fan-out lag -> scale workers (auto)
 gateway RAM -> pre-provision 2x
 Redis CPU  -> reshard online
 Postgres hot shard -> re-key (workspace_id, conv_id)
 FCM quota  -> pre-negotiate, fallback to email
```

### Q4. A misconfigured deploy pushes a bad message format that crashes all iOS clients on receipt. How do you recover?
**Answer:** This is a "poison message" incident. Immediate steps: (1) **Stop the bleeding** — pause the fan-out worker (Kafka consumer stop) so no more bad messages are delivered. The bad messages are in Postgres and Kafka but not yet on devices. (2) **Identify the bad messages** — query Postgres for messages with the offending format (e.g., `type = 99` or `body LIKE '%<bad>%'`). (3) **Quarantine** — set a `quarantined=true` flag on these rows; the Message Service / fan-out worker skips them. (4) **Deploy a client hotfix** — push an app update via App Store expedited review (or use a remote-config flag the client fetches on launch to ignore the bad `type`). (5) **Replay safe messages** — once the client fix is rolled out, un-quarantine and replay via a one-off Kafka producer. (6) For clients already crashed: they will reconnect on next app launch and fetch history; the bad message will still be in history — the client hotfix must handle it gracefully (skip unknown types). Post-mortem: add schema-registry validation on the message-produce path and a client-side "unknown type → ignore, don't crash" policy.
**Visual:**
```
1. pause fan-out (Kafka consumer stop)
2. UPDATE messages SET quarantined=true WHERE type=99
3. client hotfix (ignore unknown type) -- App Store expedited
4. remote-config flag: client drops type=99 on read
5. unpause fan-out, replay quarantined-but-now-safe messages
```

### Q5. The Redis Session Registry cluster goes down entirely. What is the user impact and how do you mitigate?
**Answer:** Without Session Registry, the fan-out worker cannot look up which gateway holds a recipient. Immediate impact: messages from online users still get written to Postgres (the write path doesn't need Redis) but **real-time delivery stops** — recipients see messages only on next poll/refresh. Mitigations: (1) Gateway has a local in-memory registry of its own connections, and gateways gossip via SWIM (HashiCorp memberlist) so the fan-out worker can query any gateway, which forwards to the right peer. (2) Clients fall back to long-polling `GET /messages?since_seq=N` every 2 s if no WebSocket frame received for 10 s. (3) Push notifications still work (they don't need Session Registry). (4) Redis Cluster should be RF=3 with automatic failover — a full-cluster outage means all 3 replicas died, which is a major incident; restore from AOF backup (Redis persistence enabled every 1 s). Recovery time: 5–10 min to restart cluster + warm cache. SLA breach but no data loss (Postgres is source of truth).
**Visual:**
```
Redis down:
  write path OK (Postgres)
  realtime delivery -> gateways gossip (SWIM) to find peers
  clients long-poll fallback (2s)
  push notifications still work
  recovery: Redis RF=3 failover, AOF restore (5-10 min)
```

### Q6. You need to add a "delete message for everyone" feature (like WhatsApp's "This message was deleted"). How do you implement it?
**Answer:** Requirements: delete within 1 hour of send, propagate to all recipients and all their devices, replace content with a tombstone. Implementation: (1) API `POST /messages/{msg_id}/delete-for-everyone` — server checks `now - created_at < 3600 s` and `sender_id == requester`. (2) Soft-delete in Postgres: `UPDATE messages SET type=99, body=NULL, deleted_at=now() WHERE msg_id=$1` — preserves the row for audit but nulls content. (3) Publish a `delete` event to Kafka `messages` topic with the same `conv_id` partition — fan-out worker delivers `{"type":"msg_deleted","msg_id":N}` to all recipients' gateways. (4) Clients receive the event and replace the message bubble with "This message was deleted". (5) Media: also delete S3 object (lifecycle: mark, then async delete after 30-day audit window). (6) Edge case: offline recipients — when they reconnect and fetch history, they get the tombstone row. (7) Search index: ES must be updated to remove the body — re-index that document or delete it. (8) Compliance: retain deleted-message metadata for 90 days for legal/abuse investigations.
**Visual:**
```
sender -> DELETE -> validate (1h, owner)
                 -> UPDATE messages SET body=NULL, deleted_at=now()
                 -> Kafka event {type: msg_deleted, msg_id}
                 -> fan-out -> clients swap bubble -> "deleted"
                 -> S3 media delete (async, 30d audit hold)
                 -> ES index update (remove body)
```

### Q7. A regulated customer (bank) wants all chat messages auditable and tamper-evident for 7 years. How do you extend the design?
**Answer:** Add a separate **audit pipeline**: (1) Every message produce also writes an immutable append-only record to S3 with object-lock (WORM) — `s3://audit/{workspace_id}/{YYYY}/{MM}/{msg_id}.json` containing the full message + signature. (2) Each record is hashed (SHA-256) and the hash is chained to the previous record's hash (Merkle-style chain) so tampering is detectable. (3) Postgres remains the operational store; S3 object-lock is the audit store. (4) Retention: S3 lifecycle moves objects to Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days (cheapest), retains 7 years. (5) Audit API: `GET /audit/export?workspace_id=W&from=&to=` — generates a signed manifest of object keys + hashes; external auditor downloads and verifies the chain. (6) Compliance: access to audit store is via a separate IAM role with break-glass logging; no normal service can delete. (7) Cost: 5 B msg/day × 1 KB × 7 years = ~12 PB on Glacier Deep Archive ≈ $12 M over 7 years — bill the regulated customer appropriately. (8) Legal hold: per-user litigation-hold flag prevents any deletion even if user requests GDPR erasure (legal-hold supersedes).
**Visual:**
```
msg produce -> Postgres (operational)
           -> S3 object-lock (WORM, hash-chained)
           -> Glacier Deep Archive @ 30d, 7y retention
audit: GET /audit/export -> manifest of (key, hash, prev_hash) -> verify chain
legal hold flag -> supersedes GDPR erasure
```
